<reason>Both sides were disciplined and well-matched, but CON held the cleaner path to victory. PRO's strongest route—CON has no mechanism that would ever say yes—was directly neutralized when CON named a concrete falsification metric (incremental health/education outcomes per public dollar over full lifetime cost, B4.1). PRO then mischaracterized that honest answer as a "concession," but CON had demanded demonstrated public value from its opening, so the framing was overclaimed, and CON's closing (B5.1) rebutted it squarely: agreeing on a spending test is not showing the spending passes it. CON also landed two real catches: PRO's own alternative-spending test was restricted to "the same communities," insulating the subsidy from national opportunity cost, and PRO's admission that taxpayers carry open-ended maintenance shortfalls came with no scale estimate. PRO answered pressure honestly (subscription-linked design, taxpayer support analogy to universal telephone service) and its auction defense ("distance sets a floor; competition determines whether we pay the floor or a monopoly premium") was sharp, but its decisive clash—commercial viability versus outcomes—resolved in CON's favor once CON showed the burden of demonstrating priority remained unmet.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was PRO's Rebuttal 2 asymmetry claim ("my opponent refused to name any benefit or metric that would ever justify paying") followed by CON's B4.1, which named a concrete per-dollar outcomes metric, and CON's closing B5.1 dismantling PRO's "concession" framing: permission to subsidize justified projects is not itself a reason to subsidize rural expansion. CON's B4.5 catch that PRO's falsification test was bounded to "the same communities," excluding national opportunity cost, was the sharpest substantive blow of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
